analysis.one_liner: Let merchants band together to negotiate the "swipe" fees banks charge on credit and debit card purchases.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it sat in the House Judiciary Committee until the 111th Congress ended, despite holding hearings in April 2010.
analysis.plain_summary: When you swipe a credit or debit card, the store pays an interchange fee to the bank that issued your card — a fee set almost entirely by banks and card networks, which merchants are largely powerless to negotiate. This bill would have let merchants collectively bargain over those fees by giving them a temporary exemption from antitrust laws, required the biggest banks to open their cost books, and forced any agreed rates to be filed publicly with the Attorney General. It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and never received a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Merchants of every size — from big retailers to small shops — would gain negotiating power over the swipe fees they pay on card transactions, and they would no longer pay higher rates than the largest merchants. Consumers would benefit indirectly if merchants passed fee savings into lower prices, which is how merchants promoted the idea.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Merchants, and shoppers if savings were passed on

how_it_helps.text: It gave merchants legal protection to band together and negotiate the fees banks and card networks charge them to accept cards, which normally antitrust law forbids.
It required the biggest banks and card networks to disclose their itemized costs and to file any negotiated agreement with the Attorney General, with the terms made public.

It required the negotiated rates to be the same for all merchants regardless of size, so small shops would pay the same rate as big chains, and it let small banks and credit unions under $1 billion in assets opt out.

analysis.who_pays: Banks that issue credit and debit cards and the card networks (Visa, Mastercard), which would have to negotiate rates with merchants collectively instead of setting them unilaterally. Rewards programs funded by interchange fees could shrink.

drawbacks.text: If negotiated rates cut interchange fees, banks said they would likely recoup the loss by reducing card rewards, annual-fee waivers, or other cardholder benefits — so some consumers could end up paying in other ways.

The nondiscrimination rule would require identical rates for every merchant regardless of transaction volume, which critics argued could raise costs for small merchants or produce rates set by the largest retailers rather than true market pricing.

The bill would have put the Justice Department in the room for every negotiation and required public filing of pricing agreements, a heavy-handed process an honest supporter would acknowledge carries its own risks of rigidity and litigation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit was lower "swipe" fees on every card purchase, savings merchants could pass to consumers; the main drawbacks are the loss of card-reward subsidies (banks might scale back points and cash back), the risk that one-size-fits-all rates shift costs onto small merchants or consumers in other ways, and the heavy DOJ-supervised process involved. Those are real trade-offs, but the bill never advanced far enough for them to be tested.

outcome.mechanism: The House Judiciary Committee held hearings on it in April 2010 but never approved it or sent it to the floor, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Representative John Conyers introduced the bill on June 4, 2009, and it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee, which he chaired.
It drew 17 cosponsors, a bipartisan group of 13 Democrats and 4 Republicans.
The committee held hearings on April 27 and 28, 2010, but the record shows no markup, no committee vote, and no House floor action.
No further action was taken before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011, so the bill expired.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit card issuers and the card networks, which kept the power to set swipe fees without facing collective merchant bargaining. Retailers and card users gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Banks and card networks kept fee-setting power

for.name: John Conyers, Jr.
for.role: U.S. Representative (MI), Chairman of the House Judiciary Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and, as Judiciary chairman, held committee hearings on it in April 2010 but never brought it to a committee vote.

for.name: Bill Shuster
for.what_they_did: Joined Conyers as the bill's Republican original cosponsor.

for.name: 13 of 253 House Democrats and 4 of 178 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it bipartisan but modest support.

against.name: Banking and credit card industry
against.role: Banks, credit unions, and card networks
against.what_they_did: Opposed legislation letting merchants collectively negotiate interchange fees, which would cut a major revenue stream; the bill's core concept was also advanced again in the 2010 financial regulation law's Durbin Amendment, which banks fought hard before losing on debit cards.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had bipartisan sponsorship (13 Democrats and 4 Republicans), but the Congress ended before any vote revealed where the parties stood.

industries.note: The bill would have let merchants collectively negotiate down the interchange fees banks collect on every card purchase, directly threatening a large, reliable revenue stream. It never came to a vote, so banks lost nothing.

industries.industry: Card networks (Visa, Mastercard and similar systems)
industries.note: Their pricing of network access would have been exposed to collective negotiation, mandatory cost disclosure, and public filing with the Justice Department. The bill died before any of this took effect.

Retailers pay interchange fees on every card sale and pass those costs into prices. The bill would have given them negotiating power and a same-rate-for-all rule, but it never advanced, so they gained nothing.
The bill let issuers with under $1 billion in assets opt out of the negotiations entirely, shielding them from any negotiated rate cuts while large banks bore the impact.
